cases.must_cite: already on empagliflozin — dapagliflozin is a second SGLT2 inhibitor
cases.stem: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 30%) is on empagliflozin, sacubitril/valsartan, and carvedilol. She reports good adherence. Her HbA1c is 7.2%. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her management?
options: Add sitagliptin to improve glycemic control
Add pioglitazone to improve glycemic control
Add dapagliflozin to further reduce heart failure risk
Increase carvedilol dose for heart failure

cases.must_cite: metformin is dose-reduced not stopped at eGFR >=30
cases.stem: A 65-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 15 years and stage 3b chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m2) has persistent albuminuria (UACR 500 mg/g) despite lisinopril 20 mg. HbA1c 8.2. She takes metformin 500 mg twice daily and glimepiride 2 mg daily. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to her diabetes regimen?
options: Continue current regimen and recheck HbA1c in 3 months
Stop metformin and start an SGLT2 inhibitor

cases.must_cite: hyperkalaemia causes peaked T via altered/accelerated repolarisation, not 'delayed repolarisation'
cases.stem: A 68-year-old man with CKD stage 3 and hypertension presents with 3 days of oliguria and dyspnea. Bilateral crackles and pitting edema. ECG reveals peaked T waves in the precordial leads. Potassium 6.8 mmol/L, creatinine 320 umol/L (baseline 150), bicarbonate 16. Which of the following best explains the ECG finding?
options: Volume overload causing left ventricular strain
Metabolic acidosis causing increased intracellular potassium shift

cases.must_cite: already on empagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor); dapagliflozin is a second SGLT2 inhibitor
cases.note: R2-UNIT test (not the R1-gate test): R2 independently returns valid=false naming empagliflozin/dapagliflozin duplication — CONFIRMED working. But this item FAILS R1 (an SGLT2i is indicated per-domain, so neither domain is load-bearing), so it cannot prove 'R1 pass -> R2 reject'. Kept as the R2 redundancy unit-test.
cases.stem: A 70-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 28%) and cardiorenal syndrome is admitted with worsening congestion. He is already established on empagliflozin, sacubitril/valsartan, spironolactone, and bisoprolol. During decongestion his creatinine rises modestly with a rising haematocrit (haemoconcentration), his potassium is 4.6 mmol/L, and his blood pressure remains tolerant. Interpreting his renal trajectory as effective decongestion rather than injury, the team wishes to further reduce his heart-failure mortality by optimising guideline-directed therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition?
options: Add dapagliflozin for additional cardiorenal protection
Add ivabradine if he is in sinus rhythm with a heart rate above 70
Add candesartan on top of sacubitril/valsartan

cases.currently: FAILING — R1 passes but R2 valid=true (misses beta-blocker duplication). This is the open V1.8.1 risk.
cases.must_cite: already on carvedilol (a beta-blocker); adding propranolol is a second beta-blocker — switch, do not add
cases.note: THE decisive R1-gate test. Genuinely integrated (thyrotoxic AF driving adrenergic tone + HFrEF constraining agents — R1 passes, both domains load-bearing). Keyed answer adds propranolol while patient is already on carvedilol. R2 must catch the beta-blocker duplication. Stable miss across 3 runs: R2 anchors on propranolol's real thyrotoxic rationale and does not enumerate carvedilol as the same class. Gate for V1.8.1 = this returns R1 pass + R2 valid=false naming carvedilol/propranolol.
cases.stem: A 44-year-old woman with newly diagnosed Graves thyrotoxicosis presents with palpitations from new atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 130. She was diagnosed 8 months ago with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 35%) and is established on carvedilol, sacubitril/valsartan and eplerenone. Her thyrotoxic state is driving heightened adrenergic tone and the arrhythmia, while her reduced ejection fraction constrains which rate-controlling agents are safe. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to control her ventricular rate?
options: Add propranolol for adrenergic rate control

cases.note: FALSE-POSITIVE CONTROL for STEP 1c v2. Patient on the correct 4-pillar HFrEF regimen minus an SGLT2 inhibitor; keyed answer ADDS empagliflozin — a DIFFERENT class from the existing agents, the guideline-endorsed 4th pillar, NOT duplication. R2 must NOT flag redundancy here. If R2 calls this a duplication, the class rule has become too broad.
cases.must_cite: empagliflozin is a distinct class (SGLT2i) completing 4-pillar therapy — not duplicative
cases.stem: A 66-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 30%) and type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 46) remains mildly symptomatic (NYHA II) despite being established and up-titrated on sacubitril/valsartan, bisoprolol and spironolactone. Potassium is 4.4 mmol/L and blood pressure is 118/72. Which of the following additions is most appropriate to further reduce his heart-failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular mortality?

note2: #V18-3 is subtle: the DIAGNOSIS (hyperkalaemia) is right but the MECHANISM wording is wrong. R2 should flag the mechanism inaccuracy. If R2 passes it because the association is correct, that is an acceptable-but-noted softer miss — the harder acceptance bar is V18-1 and V18-2 (unambiguous).
